---
title: "DATA 606 | Lab 5B · Confidence intervals"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
---


```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE)
library(infer)
set.seed(1234)
p <- 0.62
population <- rep(c("Yes", "No"), c(62000, 38000))
samp <- data.frame(climate_change_affects = sample(population, 60))
p_hat <- mean(samp$climate_change_affects == "Yes")
boot <- samp |>
  specify(response = climate_change_affects, success = "Yes") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "prop")
interval <- function(level) get_confidence_interval(boot, level = level)
ci_text <- function(ci) sprintf("%.1f%% to %.1f%%", 100 * ci[[1]], 100 * ci[[2]])
captures <- function(ci) ci[[1]] <= p && p <= ci[[2]]
simulate_intervals <- function(level, n = 60, reps = 1000, trials = 50) {
  sizes <- rhyper(trials, 62000, 38000, n)
  # Conditional on the original sample, bootstrap Yes counts are binomial.
  bounds <- t(vapply(sizes, function(x) {
    quantile(rbinom(reps, n, x / n) / n, c((1 - level) / 2, (1 + level) / 2))
  }, numeric(2)))
  data.frame(low = bounds[, 1], high = bounds[, 2],
             covers = bounds[, 1] <= p & p <= bounds[, 2])
}
show_intervals <- function(result, level) {
  i <- seq_len(nrow(result))
  plot(NA, xlim = range(c(result$low, result$high, p)), ylim = range(i),
       xlab = "Proportion answering Yes", ylab = "Sample number",
       main = paste0(100 * level, "% bootstrap confidence intervals"))
  abline(v = p, lty = 2)
  segments(result$low, i, result$high, i, lwd = ifelse(result$covers, 1, 3))
}
```

## 1–2. Point estimate

**1.** `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * p_hat)` of the sample answered Yes.

**2.** Another random sample may yield a different value. The estimates should
generally be similar because they come from the same population and both use
60 observations. The theoretical standard error is about 6.3 percentage points.

## 3–5. Interpreting confidence

```{r}
ci95 <- interval(0.95)
ci95
```

**3.** With repeated samples and the same interval construction method, we
expect about 95% of the intervals to capture the true population proportion.

**4.** My 95% interval is `r ci_text(ci95)`.
It `r if (captures(ci95)) "contains" else "does not contain"` the true 62%.
A neighbor's interval can be checked against 0.62 using the same rule.

**5.** We expect approximately 95% coverage because the method is designed for
that long-run rate. The bootstrap percentile method has approximate coverage.

## 6. Fifty intervals at 95%

```{r}
run95 <- simulate_intervals(0.95)
show_intervals(run95, 0.95)
mean(run95$covers)
```

The coverage in this run is `r 100 * mean(run95$covers)`%. Coverage varies across
runs. With 50 intervals it changes in two-percentage-point increments, so it
cannot equal 95% exactly.

## More practice

**1.** A 90% interval should be narrower because it retains less of the central
bootstrap distribution.

```{r}
ci90 <- interval(0.90)
run90 <- simulate_intervals(0.90)
show_intervals(run90, 0.90)
```

**2.** The 90% interval is `r ci_text(ci90)` for the proportion of adults in the
lab population who believe climate change affects their local community.

**3.** The plot shows all 50 intervals. Observed coverage is
`r 100 * mean(run90$covers)`%, compared with the nominal 90%.

**4.** A 99% interval should be wider than both previous intervals. With the
same sample, the 99% interval is `r ci_text(interval(0.99))`, interpreted using
the same long-run definition of confidence for the Yes proportion.

```{r}
run99 <- simulate_intervals(0.99)
show_intervals(run99, 0.99)
mean(run99$covers)
```

**5.** Larger original samples produce narrower intervals on average because
the standard error decreases.

```{r}
sapply(c(30, 60, 150), function(n) {
  result <- simulate_intervals(0.95, n = n)
  mean(result$high - result$low)
})
```

**6.** More bootstrap resamples improve the stability of the estimated bounds.
The underlying standard error is determined by the original sample size and
the response variability.

```{r}
sapply(c(100, 1000, 10000), function(reps) {
  widths <- replicate(30, {
    x <- rbinom(reps, 60, p_hat) / 60
    diff(quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975)))
  })
  c(mean_width = mean(widths), variability_of_width = sd(widths))
})
```
